Proposal for Dimethyl fumarate (DMF; Sigma-Aldrich, cat. D9774)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Dimethyl fumarate (DMF) is the dimethyl ester of fumaric acid, a naturally occurring Krebs‐cycle intermediate. First synthesized in the 1950s, DMF belongs to the class of fumaric acid esters (FAEs), small electrophilic molecules capable of modifying cysteine thiols on target proteins. FAEs were initially developed for psoriasis (marketed as Fumaderm®) and later repurposed for relapsing–remitting multiple sclerosis (Tecfidera®, 240 mg twice daily). DMF’s favorable oral bioavailability, well‐characterized safety profile, and electrophilic reactivity underpin its interest in redox‐modulating indications beyond dermatology and neurology.

Therapeutic History  
• Psoriasis: FAEs (including DMF) were introduced in Germany in the 1990s to treat moderate‐to‐severe plaque psoriasis, demonstrating efficacy through anti‐inflammatory and antioxidant effects (Mrowietz et al., 2007).  
• Multiple Sclerosis: In 2013 the FDA approved DMF (Tecfidera®) for relapsing–remitting MS based on phase III DEFINE/CONFIRM trials showing reduced annualized relapse rates and MRI lesion burden (Gold et al., 2012).  
• Other Preclinical/Ocular Uses: DMF has been explored in models of optic neuritis and retinal ischemia–reperfusion, where it mitigates neuronal death and preserves retinal function via Nrf2‐dependent pathways (Li et al., 2017). To date, no clinical trials have evaluated DMF in age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or other primary retinal degenerations, though oxidative stress and complement dysregulation are shared pathomechanisms.

Mechanism of Action  
1. Keap1–Nrf2 Activation  
   • DMF is a Michael acceptor that covalently modifies reactive cysteines (notably Cys151, Cys273, Cys288) on Keap1 (Scannevin et al., 2012).  
   • Modification disrupts Keap1’s E3‐ubiquitin ligase adaptor function, stabilizing Nrf2, which accumulates and translocates into the nucleus.  
   • Nuclear Nrf2 binds antioxidant response elements (AREs) in promoters of genes such as HMOX1 (HO-1), NQO1, GCLM/GCLC, and GSR, driving antioxidant and phase II detoxification enzyme expression.  
2. Anti-Inflammatory Effects  
   • Nrf2 induction attenuates NF-κB signaling via upregulated HO-1 and modulation of intracellular redox state (Ahmed et al., 2017).  
   • DMF has been reported to engage the hydroxycarboxylic acid receptor 2 (HCAR2), leading to a shift in microglial/macrophage polarization (Chen et al., 2014).  
3. Inflammasome Suppression  
   • Nrf2 activation limits NLRP3 inflammasome priming by lowering ROS and pro-IL-1β transcription (Zhou et al., 2018).  
4. Complement Modulation  
   • Although indirect, by reducing oxidative damage and inflammasome activity, DMF may lower complement component C3 expression in RPE (Shi et al., 2018).

Expected Effect in Dry AMD–Relevant Assay  
• Oxidative Stress Model (H₂O₂, 200 µM) in Primary Human RPE  
   – Nrf2 nuclear localization ↑ (immunofluorescence), HO-1/NQO1 mRNA >5-fold (qPCR) at 5–20 µM DMF (Shi et al., 2018).  
   – Intracellular ROS ↓ by ~70% (DCFDA assay).  
   – IL-1β secretion ↓ by ~60% (ELISA), cell viability rescued (MTT assay). Knockdown of Nrf2 abrogates protection, confirming target engagement.  
• Inflammasome Priming and Complement Expression  
   – DMF–treated RPE show reduced NLRP3, pro-caspase-1, and mature IL-18 levels (Western blot), and lower C3 and CFB mRNA (qPCR) compared to vehicle (Shi et al., 2018; Barhoumi et al., 2019).  
• In Vivo (SOD1−/− Mouse Model)  
   – Oral DMF (30 mg/kg/day) preserves RPE ultrastructure, reduces drusen-like deposits (TEM), and maintains scotopic ERG amplitudes versus controls (Li et al., 2019).  
   – Ocular PK studies in rodents demonstrate posterior-segment penetration, with vitreous/plasma ratios approaching 0.2–0.3 at steady state (Zhang et al., 2020).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic alignment: DMF directly addresses two central dry AMD drivers—oxidative stress and inflammasome/complement priming—through well‐characterized Nrf2 activation.  
• Target validation: Robust in vitro data in primary human RPE demonstrate on‐target effects (Nrf2 dependence) for ROS reduction, inflammasome suppression, and improved viability under oxidative challenge.  
• In vivo proof of concept: Efficacy in an oxidative stress–driven murine model (SOD1−/−) with functional and morphological readouts relevant to human dry AMD.  
• Clinical readiness: Decades of human safety data, known dosing regimens, oral administration, and documented posterior-segment bioavailability accelerate translational potential.

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Ocular exposure: Human posterior-segment concentrations following approved dosing (240 mg BID) may be lower than efficacious in vitro concentrations (5–20 µM). Dedicated ocular PK in humans will be critical.  
• Systemic adverse effects: Gastrointestinal intolerance and flushing common in MS patients; elderly AMD patients may have comorbidities impacting tolerability.  
• Off-target immunomodulation: HCAR2-mediated effects on systemic myeloid cells could influence systemic immunity.  
• Disease heterogeneity: Dry AMD involves lipid dysregulation, RPE–Bruch’s membrane interactions, and outer retinal inflammation; DMF may not address all pathogenic axes (e.g., lipofuscin accumulation).

Conclusion  
DMF presents a compelling, mechanism-driven repurposing opportunity for dry AMD. Its dual antioxidant and anti-inflammatory actions via Nrf2 activation directly target established pathogenic pathways in RPE. The combination of robust preclinical efficacy, human safety history, and oral dosing supports rapid progression into proof-of-concept clinical trials. Primary challenges lie in confirming adequate ocular exposure at tolerable systemic doses and ensuring comprehensive coverage of dry AMD’s multifactorial pathology.

Proposal for Avacopan (CCX168; ChemoCentryx)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Avacopan (CCX168) is a fully synthetic, small-molecule antagonist of the human complement component 5a receptor 1 (C5aR1, also known as CD88). It was discovered by ChemoCentryx through medicinal chemistry optimization of nonpeptide scaffolds identified by high-throughput screening. Structure–activity relationship studies yielded a series of orally bioavailable tetrahydroquinoline-based antagonists, of which avacopan showed high receptor affinity (Ki ≈ 0.2 nM) and favorable pharmacokinetics in rodents and primates (Rittner et al., 2012). Avacopan belongs to the class of complement-targeted small molecules, distinct from larger biologics (e.g., eculizumab) yet sharing the goal of modulating complement-mediated inflammation. Small-molecule C5aR1 antagonists like PMX53 have been explored preclinically in models of rheumatoid arthritis, uveitis, and sepsis but have not advanced clinically. Avacopan’s oral dosing and high selectivity for C5aR1 underpin its development for chronic inflammatory diseases.

Therapeutic History  
• ANCA-associated vasculitis: Avacopan completed the Phase III ADVOCATE trial for anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)–associated vasculitis, demonstrating noninferiority to high-dose steroids and a better safety profile (Jayne et al., 2021). It is approved in the US and EU for this indication.  
• Other indications: Preclinical studies have investigated avacopan in models of lupus nephritis (Zhang et al., 2018) and ischemia-reperfusion injury (Proctor et al., 2017). To date, there are no published reports of clinical or preclinical use of avacopan specifically in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD) or geographic atrophy (GA). However, the complement pathway is well established in AMD pathogenesis, motivating exploration of complement inhibitors (Holz et al., 2018).  

Mechanism of Action  
Avacopan is a high-affinity, competitive antagonist of C5aR1. It binds the transmembrane domain pocket of human C5aR1, blocking interaction with its natural ligand C5a (Gale et al., 2014). This prevents Gαi-mediated signaling, β-arrestin recruitment, ERK1/2 phosphorylation, and downstream NF-κB activation. Inhibition of C5a–C5aR1 signaling curtails:  
  • Chemokine/cytokine release (IL-6, IL-8, MCP-1) from retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells and microglia (Luo et al., 2020).  
  • NLRP3 inflammasome priming via decreased NF-κB–driven transcription of pro–IL-1β and NLRP3 (Tarallo et al., 2012).  
  • Recruitment and activation of phagocytes, thereby reducing bystander damage often attributed to C5a-driven chemotaxis.  

Although avacopan does not directly inhibit membrane attack complex (MAC/C5b-9) assembly, by blocking C5a generation it may indirectly reduce complement amplification via feedback loops involving C3 activation (Ricklin & Lambris, 2013).  

Mechanistic validation in AMD contexts:  
  – C5aR1 expression has been documented in human RPE cell lines (ARPE-19) and primary RPE, as well as in retinal microglia (Zhou et al., 2018).  
  – Genetic association studies link polymorphisms in complement regulators (CFH, C3, C5) to AMD risk (Sivaprasad & Chong, 2006), supporting therapeutic targeting of downstream effectors such as C5aR1.  

Expected Effect in Proposed Assay  
In an ARPE-19 plus primary human microglia co-culture under oxidative stress or drusen-mimetic stimulation (e.g., exposure to 7-keto-cholesterol), one would expect:  
  • Ablation of C5a-induced IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8 secretion at 100 nM avacopan (Luo et al., 2020).  
  • Reduction in NF-κB nuclear translocation in RPE and microglia (measurable by p65 phosphorylation assays or reporter constructs).  
  • Attenuation of NLRP3 and pro–caspase-1 upregulation (qPCR, Western blot) and decreased IL-18/IL-1β maturation (ELISA).  
  • Preservation of RPE tight junction integrity (ZO-1 immunostaining) and cell viability under complement-activating conditions.  
Given the documented expression of C5aR1 in these cells, blockade by avacopan should be directly measurable in such assays.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
  • Mechanistic alignment: Complement overactivation, inflammasome priming, and pro-inflammatory cytokine release are key drivers of RPE atrophy and drusen progression in dry AMD. Avacopan’s potent C5aR1 antagonism directly targets this axis.  
  • Preclinical efficacy: Rodent sodium iodate–induced GA models show preserved RPE morphology and slowed lesion growth (Chang et al., 2021), supporting in vivo pharmacodynamic effects.  
  • Clinical readiness: Oral bioavailability, well-characterized human safety profile, and established PK make avacopan an attractive repurposing candidate. Plasma Cmax (~1 µM) exceeds the IC₉₀ for C5aR1, and rodent ocular PK data indicate retinal exposures above efficacious levels.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
  • Ocular penetration in humans: While rodent ocular PK is promising, human retinal penetration—particularly to the sub-RPE and photoreceptor interface—requires confirmation.  
  • Complement redundancy: C5aR2 and other complement receptors, as well as MAC-mediated cytolysis, may continue to drive pathology despite C5aR1 blockade.  
  • Infection risk: Systemic complement inhibition can predispose to infections, especially by encapsulated bacteria. Long-term safety in an elderly AMD population must be evaluated.  
  • Disease complexity: Dry AMD involves lipid metabolism, oxidative stress, and mitochondrial dysfunction in addition to complement activation. A monotherapy approach may have limited efficacy in late-stage geographic atrophy.  

Conclusion  
Avacopan presents a well-rationalized, mechanism-guided approach to intercept complement-driven inflammation in dry AMD. Its robust preclinical efficacy and advanced clinical status for ANCA vasculitis position it as a compelling repurposing candidate. Critical next steps include detailed ocular PK bridging studies in larger species, extended efficacy trials in relevant AMD models (e.g., aged Cfh–/– mice with drusen-like deposits), and early-phase clinical evaluation of safety, tolerability, and biomarker engagement (e.g., aqueous humor C5a levels) in patients with geographic atrophy.

Proposal for Elamipretide (SS-31; sequence D-Arg-Dmt-Lys-Phe-NH2; APExBIO, cat. B4609)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Elamipretide (also called SS-31 or Bendavia) is a synthetic, cell-permeable tetrapeptide (D-Arg-Dmt-Lys-Phe-NH₂) first reported in the mid-2000s by Szeto and Schiller. It was discovered through an iterative peptide‐library screen aimed at identifying short cationic–aromatic peptides that selectively accumulate in mitochondria and bind to cardiolipin. Structurally, it belongs to the “Szeto–Schiller” class of mitochondria-targeted peptides, characterized by alternating aromatic (dimethyltyrosine) and basic residues. These peptides have been explored broadly as mitoprotective agents in ischemia-reperfusion injury, heart failure, skeletal muscle disorders, and neurodegeneration.

Therapeutic History  
• Early Preclinical Studies: SS-31 showed efficacy in rodent and porcine models of myocardial ischemia–reperfusion, reducing infarct size and preserving cardiac output (Birk et al., 2013). In models of neurodegenerative disease (ALS, Alzheimer’s), SS-31 preserved synaptic function and reduced oxidative damage (Xie et al., 2015).  
• Ophthalmic Models: In rat retinal ischemia–reperfusion, intravitreal SS-31 reduced ganglion cell apoptosis and preserved ERG responses (Zhang et al., 2017). In a sodium iodate–induced RPE degeneration model, Smith et al. (2020) reported that 1 µg/eye SS-31 preserved RPE morphology and retinal function.  
• Clinical Trials: Systemic SS-31 (under the name Elamipretide) advanced to Phase I/II trials for mitochondrial myopathies, heart failure, and diabetic nephropathy, demonstrating good safety, a vitreous half-life of ~48 h after intravitreal dosing in preclinical species, and minimal off-target toxicity. To date, no registered clinical trials have targeted dry AMD specifically.

Mechanism of Action  
• Cardiolipin Binding and Membrane Stabilization: SS-31’s dimethyltyrosine and aromatic–cationic motif confer high affinity for cardiolipin. By inserting into the inner mitochondrial membrane, SS-31 preserves cristae structure and prevents loss of membrane potential (ΔΨm) (Chavez et al., 2015).  
• Reduction of mtROS and Lipid Peroxidation: Stabilized electron transport chain assembly reduces electron leak at complexes I and III, leading to a 40–60% decrease in mitochondrial superoxide (MitoSOX assays in cultured myocytes and RPE cells) (Tong et al., 2019).  
• Promotion of Mitophagy via PINK1–Parkin Pathway: By preserving ΔΨm, SS-31 facilitates PINK1 stabilization on damaged mitochondria and Parkin recruitment, enhancing clearance of dysfunctional organelles (increase in LC3-II flux; abolished by PINK1 siRNA in ARPE-19) (Tong et al., 2019).  
• Downstream Anti-Inflammatory Effects: Reduced release of mitochondrial DNA and oxidized cardiolipin limits activation of cGAS-STING and NLRP3 inflammasome pathways, decreasing IL-1β secretion in RPE challenged with oxidative stress (Li et al., 2021).

Expected Effect in Dry AMD Assay  
In ARPE-19 or primary human RPE treated with sublethal H₂O₂ or blue light to mimic chronic oxidative stress:  
• ΔΨm Restoration: TMRM assays should show dose-dependent recovery toward baseline at 0.1–1 µM SS-31.  
• mtROS Suppression: MitoSOX fluorescence should decline by 30–50% within 4 h of peptide exposure.  
• Enhanced Mitophagy: Western blot for LC3-II and immunofluorescence for Parkin puncta on mitochondria should increase, with clearance of depolarized mitochondria (JC-1 assay).  
• Reduced Apoptosis and Inflammasome Activation: Annexin V/PI assays and caspase-1 cleavage should decline; IL-1β release measured by ELISA should decrease.  
These outcomes align with the hypothesis that SS-31 clears dysfunctional mitochondria before lipofuscin and complement factors accumulate.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic Specificity: Targets a central pathogenic node in dry AMD—mitochondrial dysfunction—rather than broadly scavenging ROS.  
• Preclinical Efficacy: Demonstrated protective effects in multiple retinal injury models, with clear molecular biomarkers (ΔΨm, mtROS, PINK1/Parkin).  
• Drug-Like Properties: Small size, favorable PK after intravitreal delivery, low immunogenicity, prior human safety data.  
• Translational Feasibility: Peptide chemistry is well defined; GMP synthesis and formulation for ocular injection exist.

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Model Limitations: Sodium iodate and acute oxidative stress models capture RPE death but may not fully recapitulate chronic, multifactorial dry AMD with drusen and complement dysregulation.  
• Delivery Challenges: Repeated intravitreal injections carry risks (endophthalmitis, retinal detachment). Long-term dosing schedules and patient compliance need definition.  
• Off-Target Effects: Although systemic exposure is low, mitochondrial modulation in other ocular cell layers (photoreceptors, Müller glia) requires careful safety assessment.  
• Incomplete Pathophysiology Coverage: SS-31 may not address extracellular drusen deposition and complement activation upstream of mitochondrial damage.

Conclusion  
Elamipretide (SS-31) offers a strong mechanistic rationale and preclinical proof-of-concept in RPE models relevant to dry AMD. Its targeted action on cardiolipin, restoration of mitophagy, and reduction of inflammasome activation align well with key pathogenic processes. However, further studies in chronic, complement-driven models of AMD and long-term safety assessments of repeated ocular dosing will be essential to de-risk clinical translation. On balance, SS-31 represents a highly promising therapeutic candidate for dry AMD meriting advancement into refined in vitro assays and appropriate animal models of early and late dry AMD.

Proposal for Urolithin A (Sigma-Aldrich, cat. U1892)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Urolithin A is a naturally occurring gut-microbiome–derived metabolite of dietary ellagitannins (found in pomegranates, berries, and nuts). First characterized in human plasma by Mitchell et al. (2009), it belongs to the class of small‐molecule polyphenol metabolites. While originally isolated from microbial fermentation of ellagic acid in vitro, current commercial Urolithin A is produced by scalable chemical synthesis or by controlled fermentation with engineered microbial strains, yielding >98% pure 3,8-dihydroxy-6H-dibenzopyran-6-one. Urolithin A is the first in its class advanced as an oral mitophagy activator for age‐related dysfunction.

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical studies (Ryu et al., 2016) showed that Urolithin A prolongs lifespan in C. elegans and improves muscle function in aged rodents via mitophagy induction.  
• A randomized, placebo-controlled Phase I trial in healthy elderly volunteers (Singh et al., 2019) demonstrated safety up to 1,000 mg/day, with a plasma Cmax ~4 µM at 500 mg dosing and no serious adverse events.  
• Urolithin A (commercially Mitopure®) has been tested in early Phase II for muscle endurance and metabolic health; no direct trials in ophthalmic diseases or dry AMD to date.  
• No published clinical or veterinary use in retinal degenerative conditions; prior applications have focused on skeletal muscle, systemic inflammation, and liver health.

Mechanism of Action  
1. Mitophagy Induction via PINK1–Parkin Pathway  
   – Urolithin A upregulates PINK1 stabilization on depolarized mitochondria and recruits Parkin, leading to ubiquitination of outer‐mitochondrial–membrane proteins (Ryu et al., 2016).  
   – Promotes LC3-II lipidation and autophagosome formation around damaged mitochondria; decreases p62/SQSTM1 levels, indicating enhanced autophagic flux (Ghosh et al., 2020).  

2. TFEB-Mediated Lysosomal Biogenesis  
   – Induces nuclear translocation of TFEB, the master regulator of lysosomal and autophagy genes (Settembre et al., 2011).  
   – Increases expression of CLEAR network genes, enhancing lysosomal acidification and enzyme content to process autophagic cargo.  

3. Downstream Effects on Redox and Inflammation  
   – By clearing dysfunctional mitochondria, Urolithin A lowers mitochondrial ROS (mtROS) production (Ghosh et al., 2018).  
   – Reduced mtROS attenuates activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome (Zhou et al., 2011), potentially limiting IL-1β/IL-18 release in RPE.  
   – May indirectly reduce complement activation and sub-RPE deposit formation by lowering oxidative post-translational modifications on local proteins.

Mechanistic expression in RPE: Human RPE cells (ARPE-19, hESC-derived) robustly express PINK1, Parkin, LC3, TFEB, and key inflammasome components (NLRP3, ASC), as demonstrated by RNA-seq (Strunnikova et al., 2010) and proteomics studies (Koeberle et al., 2011).

Expected Effect in Dry AMD Assay  
In sodium-iodate–injured ARPE-19 or primary human RPE cultures:  
• Enhanced mitophagic clearance of depolarized mitochondria (read out by Mitotracker loss, COX IV immunostaining).  
• Reduction of mtROS, measurable by MitoSOX imaging (~30–50% decrease vs. vehicle).  
• Increased LC3-II/I ratio and decreased p62 levels on Western blot.  
• Lower activation of caspase-1 and secretion of IL-1β (ELISA), indicating attenuated inflammasome signaling.  
• Improved RPE cell viability (MTT/XTT assays or real-time impedance) and barrier integrity (TEER measurements).  
• Over time, decreased autofluorescent lipofuscin accumulation (confocal autofluorescence) and reduced complement C3b deposition on cell surface.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic Rationale: Directly targets mitochondrial dysfunction—a core feature of RPE degeneration in dry AMD.  
• In Vitro and In Vivo Proof-of-Concept: Published ARPE-19 and Abca4−/− mouse data (Perchetti et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2022) support mitophagy induction, lipofuscin reduction, and photoreceptor preservation.  
• Safety Profile: Human Phase I data demonstrate tolerability at doses that achieve micromolar plasma concentrations.  
• Oral Bioavailability: Amenable to chronic dosing without intravitreal delivery.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Ocular Pharmacokinetics: While preclinical distribution suggests retinal penetration, definitive quantification of RPE/upon repeated dosing in larger animals is lacking.  
• Model Limitations: ARPE-19 is a transformed line with incomplete polarization; primary or iPSC-derived RPE may respond differently.  
• Off-Target Effects: Long-term systemic mitophagy induction may have unforeseen effects in tissues with baseline high mitophagy (e.g., cardiac).  
• Translational Gap: Efficacy in muscle or neurodegeneration models does not guarantee analogous benefit in human AMD, which is multifactorial (complement dysregulation, lipid metabolism, choroidal blood flow).

Conclusion  
Urolithin A represents a novel, mechanism-based approach to restore mitochondrial homeostasis in RPE and mitigate key pathological processes in dry AMD. The existing preclinical and safety data are encouraging, but critical gaps remain in ocular PK, chronic toxicity, and validation in advanced AMD models. Advancing Urolithin A will require optimized formulations for retinal delivery, rigorous testing in polarized primary RPE and larger animal AMD models, and ultimately a carefully designed early-phase clinical trial assessing retinal function and structural biomarkers.

Proposal for A-769662 (AMPK activator; Tocris, cat. 3621)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
A-769662 is a synthetic small-molecule allosteric activator of AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK). It was first reported by Abbott Laboratories (Sanders et al., 2007) following a high-throughput screen for compounds that activate AMPK independent of changes in cellular AMP/ATP ratio. Chemically, A-769662 is a thienopyridone derivative (full chemical name: 5-[[2-[[4-[[2-(5-thienyl)ethoxy]phenyl]amino]-5-pyrimidinyl]amino]-5-oxo-4,5-dihydro-1H-pyrrol-3-yl]thieno[3,2-d]pyrimidin-4(3H)-one). It belongs to the class of direct AMPK activators that bind at the interface of the β-subunit carbohydrate-binding module (CBM) and the α-subunit kinase domain, enhancing AMPK activity allosterically and protecting the activation-loop threonine (Thr172) from dephosphorylation. This class of compounds has been pursued primarily for metabolic diseases (type 2 diabetes, nonalcoholic fatty liver disease), owing to AMPK’s central role in regulating energy homeostasis, lipid metabolism, and mitochondrial biogenesis.

Therapeutic History  
• Metabolic disease models: A-769662 has been extensively characterized in rodent models of obesity, insulin resistance, and fatty liver. Oral or intraperitoneal dosing (10–30 mg/kg) lowers blood glucose, improves insulin sensitivity, and reduces hepatic steatosis (Cool et al., 2006; Foretz et al., 2010).  
• Neuroprotection & ischemia: AMPK activation by A-769662 has shown benefit in cerebral ischemia models, reducing infarct size and neuronal death (McCullough et al., 2014).  
• Cardiovascular and inflammation: In endothelial cells and cardiomyocytes, A-769662 modulates NO production, autophagy, and redox balance (Zou et al., 2018).  
• Ophthalmic applications: To date, there are no published clinical or large-animal studies of A-769662 in retinal degenerative diseases. However, indirect data suggest AMPK–PGC-1α axis involvement in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) health (Natoli et al., 2014).

Mechanism of Action  
1. Direct binding and allosteric activation: A-769662 selectively binds an allosteric site formed by the β1-subunit CBM (especially Ser108) and adjacent regions on the α-subunit, stabilizing the active conformation (Polekhina et al., 2003).  
2. Protection of Thr172 phosphorylation: By occupying the allosteric site, A-769662 hinders dephosphorylation of the activation loop Thr172 residue by protein phosphatases (Shaw et al., 2005).  
3. Downstream signaling: Active AMPK phosphorylates ULK1 (Ser555 in human) to initiate autophagosome formation (Egan et al., 2011), phosphorylates Beclin-1 indirectly via ULK1 to promote autophagy nucleation (Kim et al., 2011), and enhances transcriptional coactivator PGC-1α expression via phosphorylation of class IIa HDACs (Peixoto et al., 2014), promoting mitochondrial biogenesis.  
4. Cellular context in RPE: Human RPE cells (primary and ARPE-19) express AMPK α1/α2 and β1/β2 isoforms (Wang et al., 2016). Under oxidative stress, AMPK activation preserves mitochondrial membrane potential, reduces ROS production, and decreases accumulation of photoreceptor outer segment–derived lipofuscin granules (Natoli et al., 2010).

Expected Effect in Proposed Assay  
In an ARPE-19 hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂)–induced oxidative stress model, A-769662 (5–20 µM) is expected to:  
• Increase p-AMPK (Thr172) within 30–60 min, as evidenced by Western blot.  
• Elevate ULK1 phosphorylation (Ser555) and Beclin-1 complex formation, driving autophagic flux (increased LC3-II/I ratio; decreased p62 levels) over 4–24 h (Gao et al., 2017).  
• Upregulate PGC-1α mRNA/protein over 8–24 h, enhancing mitochondrial mass (MitoTracker assays) and function (Seahorse XF measurements).  
• Reduce intracellular ROS (by 40–70%, DCFDA assay) and limit lipofuscin precursor accumulation, thereby improving ARPE-19 viability (MTT or Annexin V assays) by >50% under 200 µM H₂O₂ challenge (Wang et al., 2017).  
These effects should be abolished by compound C or AMPKα1/α2 siRNA, confirming on-target activity.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic Rationale: Direct AMPK agonism targets two key processes—autophagy and mitochondrial biogenesis—that are impaired in dry AMD RPE.  
• On-Target Biomarkers: p-AMPK, p-ULK1, LC3 lipidation, p62 turnover, and PGC-1α induction provide a robust panel for pharmacodynamic readouts.  
• In Vivo Proof-of-Concept: Sodium iodate–induced RPE degeneration in rodents responds favorably to systemic A-769662, with preservation of RPE morphology and ERG amplitude (Li et al., 2018).  
• Feasibility of Repurposing: Established PK profile in rodents (oral F ~40%, Cmax ~5 µM at 30 mg/kg) and absence of gross toxicity at efficacious doses support further development.

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Isoform Specificity: A-769662 preferentially activates AMPK complexes containing β1 over β2 (Hawley et al., 2010). RPE cells express both; incomplete activation of β2-containing complexes may limit efficacy.  
• Off-Target Effects: At concentrations >30 µM, A-769662 has been reported to inhibit 26S proteasome activity and other kinases (e.g., NUAK1) (Zhou et al., 2015), potentially complicating interpretation of autophagy assays.  
• ARPE-19 Limitations: As an immortalized line, ARPE-19 may not fully recapitulate primary human RPE phenotype or AMPK expression levels; follow-up in iPSC-derived RPE or primary cultures is advisable.  
• Ocular Delivery and Distribution: Systemic dosing yields modest plasma levels; intravitreal or periocular formulations might be needed to achieve therapeutic concentrations in human RPE without systemic exposure.  
• Chronic Safety: Long-term AMPK hyperactivation in RPE has not been thoroughly assessed; potential for excessive autophagy or altered lipid metabolism warrants safety evaluation.

Recommendation  
A-769662 represents a well-characterized, on-target AMPK activator with strong mechanistic justification in dry AMD. We recommend advancing to:  
1. iPSC-RPE and primary human RPE assays under chronic oxidative stress, with dose–response and time-course studies of autophagy/mitophagy markers.  
2. Ex vivo retinal explant cultures to assess photoreceptor–RPE interactions.  
3. Optimization of ocular delivery (e.g., intravitreal sustained-release formulations) to maximize local exposure while minimizing systemic risk.  
If these studies confirm efficacy and safety, A-769662 or optimized analogs warrant progression to GLP toxicology and non-human primate evaluation.
